newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran poll body slaps paper for backing candidate.
newsitem.headline: Iran poll body slaps paper for backing candidate.

text.p: An Iranian election body said on Monday it would file charges against a state-funded newspaper for campaigning on behalf of a presidential candidate backed by supporters of outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.

The body overseeing publicity in the May 23 election ruled that the daily Hamshahri, published by the Tehran municipality, had violated a law prohibiting state-funded papers from electioneering, state-run Tehran radio said.
Hamshahri had been accused by backers of a main conservative candidate, Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, of giving wide coverage to his leading rival, Mohammad Khatami.

The ruling was a blow to Khatami who has come under fire by hardline conservatives who have questioned his allegiance to Iran's Shi'ite Moslem clerical leadership and alleged that his campaign was backed by public funds.
Tehran's mayor, who runs the mass-circulation newspaper, is a leading figure among pro-Rafsanjani centrists who have backed Khatami, a former minister of culture and Islamic guidance.
Last week Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei asked officials to prevent state-funded newspapers from providing publicity for a particular candidate.
Iran will announce the names of approved presidential candidates on Thursday, allowing 12 days to campaign, the official news agency IRNA said on Monday.
It said the candidates were being chosen by the Guardian Council out of 238 who had signed up to run in the elections.
The Guardian Council, a powerful body of lawyers and clerics, approved only four out of 128 who signed up to run in the 1993 election.
This year's poll is shaping up as a two-horse race between Khatami and Nateq-Nouri, who has won the backing of key clerical groups. Both men are Shi'ite clerics.

Tehran residents said Khatami appeared to be gaining support among women, young people and intellectuals who fear a harder application of Islamic rules governing everyday life and restrictions of freedom of press if Nateq-Nouri is elected.

The daily Akhbar said on Monday hardline opponents of Khatami disrupted a meeting in southwestern Iran where Faezeh Hashemi, one of Rafsanjani's daughters who has been active with women's issues, was due to speak in support of the candidate.
But the clerical support for Nateq-Nouri has not been unanimous.
The daily Jomhuri Eslami said Islamic seminary students had strongly protested when the leader of a hardline group had attacked Khatami during a speech in the holy city of Qom.
The Guardian Council screens candidates for their allegiance to Iran's religious leadership and the Islamic system of government established after the 1979 revolution.

Nine women were among those who signed up in a effort to force a legal interpretation allowing female candidates to run. But election officials said they doubted that the Council would allow any women to run.
Rafsanjani is barred by the constitution from running for a third consecutive four-year term. His term ends on August 3.
